title: AI Won't Replace Junior Lawyers. It Will Give Them Better Work
pub: Bloomberg Law (bylined by the chair and managing partner of Lowenstein Sandler; mirrored on lowenstein.com)
author: Gary M. Wingens

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Wingens rejects the cluster’s principal threat framing, arguing that AI can expand demand, increase junior employment and improve junior training through copilot-style assistance. Although he conditions these benefits on independent thinking and active supervision, his overall position is that AI can strengthen rather than erode expertise reproduction.
qs: AI will create more work for firms, including our most junior lawyers, and let us deliver the services clients want at lower cost and higher quality.

On smaller matters, senior lawyers can sometimes just do the junior-level task themselves, but on the larger and more complex matters, AI makes our junior lawyers more productive while giving them something I never had, a co-pilot they can engage with to explain an unfamiliar provision or a theory of a case that will improve their training and their ultimate work product.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Wingens accepts that AI compresses routine work, affects pricing and enables some client insourcing, but rejects the cluster’s threat-centred framing. He instead argues that lower costs will expand legal demand and that AI, paired with independent judgment and supervision, will raise junior capability and move juniors into higher-value work rather than broadly flattening the pyramid.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that automation can remove junior tasks and pressure traditional development routes, then materially extends the cluster with a conditional alternative: expanding demand, earlier progression to higher-value work, active supervision and structured AI instruction could increase rather than reduce junior roles. Its claims are practitioner-based and conditional, consistent with the cluster’s view that employment and training outcomes remain unresolved.
qs: But, if demand for legal work rises faster than AI alone can absorb it, and our juniors can take on work that once demanded a more senior lawyer, a firm doesn’t need fewer junior lawyers to meet that demand.
Second, supervising lawyers must do their part by explaining how a matter is structured, sharing prompts and best use cases, and treating the technology as something to teach rather than hoard.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption changes legal economics rather than merely improving productivity, and materially extends the cluster with a project-specific example of sharply reduced client cost alongside law-firm revenue at higher hourly rates. It also develops the pricing analysis by advocating alternative fee arrangements and shared productivity gains, while forecasting demand expansion rather than straightforward revenue displacement.
qs: This past year, with AI assistance we fully disclosed, we brought the expected cost of that same project down by roughly 70%, even though our hourly rates had risen in the interim.

As these tools mature, we will share those gains with our clients not just through lower effective hours but through the faster implementation of alternative fee arrangements that tie total cost more closely to value.

His firm-level cost example and conditional forecast for junior hiring strengthen the cluster’s treatment of selected returns and contested staffing outcomes, though they do not establish market-wide effects.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wingens accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will redesign and reallocate legal work rather than replace lawyers wholesale. He materially extends it with firm-level examples, including a disclosed project with an estimated 70% cost reduction, and a Jevons-Paradox argument that lower costs may expand demand, preserve junior work and accelerate alternative fee arrangements. His labour forecast is more optimistic and less qualified than the cluster’s unsettled assessment.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Wingens supports the cluster’s core view that AI is reconfiguring legal work rather than replacing lawyers wholesale. He reports strong efficiency gains on bounded, document-intensive tasks, treats AI as a copilot for juniors, and stresses independent verification, supervision and training. He is more optimistic than the synthesis about apprenticeship and junior employment risks, predicting higher-value work and demand growth, but does not reject the need for competence safeguards.

st.an: Wingens supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI will reorganise legal production and pricing rather than eliminate lawyers. He describes bounded automation, lower project costs, insourcing of routine work, value-linked fees and continued reliance on seasoned judgment. His stronger forecast that demand growth will expand junior employment is conditional and fits the cluster’s conclusion that net employment effects remain unresolved.

kp.k: Lower costs could expand demand rather than shrink staffing
kp.d: Wingens rejects the prediction he reports hearing at leadership conferences that automation will flatten the law-firm pyramid and sharply reduce junior hiring. Drawing an analogy to Jevons's 1860s observation about coal consumption, he predicts that cheaper legal services will activate work clients previously deferred, narrowed or abandoned. This is an economic argument and forecast, not a measured staffing finding.
qs: AI will create more work for firms, including our most junior lawyers, and let us deliver the services clients want at lower cost and higher quality.
The same logic, known as the Jevons Paradox, should apply to legal services.
As work becomes faster and cheaper, clients will buy more of it, not less.

kp.k: Firm examples show automation of document-intensive tasks
kp.d: Wingens reports existing uses within his firm: large language models review trust and servicing agreements to identify obligations and support negotiations; side-letter review is largely automated across funds with hundreds of investors; and litigation teams search hundreds of deposition transcripts for passages supporting or undermining arguments. He presents these examples as evidence of falling routine-work costs alongside increasing value from surrounding judgment.
qs: First, the cost of the routine parts of legal work is falling, sometimes dramatically, even as the value of the judgment around that work keeps rising.
In structured finance, we use large language models to review high volumes of trust and servicing agreements, surfacing our clients’ obligations and strengthening our hand in negotiating deals.
In our funds practice, we have largely automated side-letter review across funds with hundreds of investors.
And in litigation and disputes, our lawyers use AI to comb through hundreds of deposition transcripts for the quote that supports, or undermines, an argument in a brief.

kp.k: One previously rejected project became viable with AI
kp.d: Wingens recounts a client project abandoned a few years earlier because of cost. In the past year, disclosed AI assistance reduced its expected cost by roughly 70%, despite intervening hourly-rate increases. He reports resulting revenue for the firm and lower-cost risk reduction for the client; the example concerns expected project cost, not a measured firm-wide saving.
qs: A few years ago, a client looked hard at a large project, saw the price tag, and decided not to proceed.
This past year, with AI assistance we fully disclosed, we brought the expected cost of that same project down by roughly 70%, even though our hourly rates had risen in the interim.
After AI, we had real revenue at higher rates and a client that had limited that risk at a far lower cost.

kp.k: Discovery savings and alternative fees could improve viability
kp.d: Wingens argues that cheaper discovery could restore the economic viability of meritorious middle-market litigation previously burdened by document-review costs in the millions. He also anticipates sharing productivity gains through fewer effective hours and faster adoption of alternative fee arrangements linking total cost to value, framing client demand as demand for solutions rather than billable time.
qs: I have never met a client who came to us looking to buy billable hours; they want solutions to their business problems, and the billable hour has long been a proxy for how we charge for those services.

The same logic, applied to discovery, can take a middle-market dispute for which document review once cost millions and dramatically bring down that cost, making an entire tier of meritorious litigation once again viable.

As these tools mature, we will share those gains with our clients not just through lower effective hours but through the faster implementation of alternative fee arrangements that tie total cost more closely to value.

kp.k: Client productivity could generate additional legal work
kp.d: Wingens predicts a second demand channel beyond cheaper legal services: AI-enabled clients will undertake more business activity. He expects fund managers to assess and negotiate more transactions, technology and life sciences businesses to generate more protectable intellectual property, and AI itself to produce disputes and eventually bankruptcy and restructuring work.
qs: The second factor that I believe will lead to increased demand for law firm services is that our clients will become more productive.
For example, the private fund managers we represent will use AI to vet more deal flow and negotiate more private equity and venture transactions each year, and more transactions mean more legal work.
Our technology and life sciences clients will generate ideas, and intellectual property worth protecting, faster than ever.
And AI itself will generate a steady stream of disputes for our litigators and ultimately create significant work for our bankruptcy and restructuring teams.

kp.k: Insourcing offsets demand, but judgment remains a differentiator
kp.d: Wingens acknowledges that in-house counsel will use the same legally trained AI tools to bring routine work inside the business, offsetting some additional external demand. He characterizes that work as high-volume and low-judgment, while arguing that expanded business activity will generate higher-stakes matters requiring seasoned lawyers and market knowledge rather than an AI agent alone.
qs: Some of these extra demands will be offset.
Our clients will have access to the same legally trained AI tools we rely on, and in-house counsel will use them to pull more routine work back inside the business.
The higher-stakes matters that follow are exactly the ones that call for seasoned judgment, not just a capable AI agent.
Knowing current market terms in private deals or which provision matters isn’t something a client can download.

kp.k: Junior staffing growth depends on demand outpacing automation
kp.d: Drawing on conversations with counsel and associates, Wingens distinguishes smaller matters, where senior lawyers may perform junior tasks themselves, from larger complex matters, where AI can augment juniors and explain unfamiliar provisions or case theories. His prediction of needing more juniors is explicitly conditional on demand rising faster than AI can absorb it and juniors taking on work previously requiring greater seniority.
qs: I asked a number of our counsel and associates how our youngest lawyers are using these tools.

On smaller matters, senior lawyers can sometimes just do the junior-level task themselves, but on the larger and more complex matters, AI makes our junior lawyers more productive while giving them something I never had, a co-pilot they can engage with to explain an unfamiliar provision or a theory of a case that will improve their training and their ultimate work product.

But, if demand for legal work rises faster than AI alone can absorb it, and our juniors can take on work that once demanded a more senior lawyer, a firm doesn’t need fewer junior lawyers to meet that demand.
It needs more of them, trained to expertly use and learn from AI tools that will allow them to take on higher-value work sooner.

kp.k: Independent thinking and active supervision condition training benefits
kp.d: Wingens makes the benefits of AI-assisted junior work contingent on juniors questioning outputs and retaining independent judgment. Supervisors must explain matter structure, share prompts and effective applications, and actively teach the technology rather than withhold their expertise.
qs: This all only works if two things happen.
First, junior lawyers must keep thinking for themselves and questioning the output.
Second, supervising lawyers must do their part by explaining how a matter is structured, sharing prompts and best use cases, and treating the technology as something to teach rather than hoard.

kp.k: Curated firm knowledge could differentiate commoditized AI
kp.d: Wingens advocates connecting juniors to the firm's curated precedent collection and tools highlighting typical deal terms and litigation strategies. He argues that access to collective proprietary knowledge offers an advantage clients cannot replicate and predicts that this knowledge will become especially important as underlying AI models become commodities.
qs: I get excited about connecting junior associates to our firm’s “golden source” of precedent, a curated store of our best documents with tools that highlight typical deal terms and litigation strategies.
An associate with that access can tap the collective knowledge of the whole firm in a way no client can replicate.
That proprietary know‑how will matter most as the underlying AI models themselves become commodities.

kp.k: Technology-native graduates could support intergenerational learning
kp.d: Over the next few years, Wingens expects graduates to become increasingly native users of AI. He invokes older lawyers' history of learning tools from younger colleagues and asserts that many current juniors bring prior work experience and sharper judgment than earlier generations, supporting his broader view that AI raises junior capability rather than simply replacing juniors.
qs: In the next few years, law school graduates will be increasingly native in this technology.
Older lawyers have always learned new tools from younger colleagues, and many of today’s junior attorneys arrive with real work experience and sharper judgment than earlier generations.
AI doesn’t so much replace the junior lawyer as raising the floor on what a junior lawyer can do, and the client is the one who benefits.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Gary M. Wingens predicts that AI-driven cost reductions will expand demand for legal services rather than simply reduce firms' work.
pts.d: Wingens, Lowenstein Sandler's chair and managing partner, rejects the prediction he reports hearing at leadership conferences that automation necessarily means fewer junior lawyers and a flatter staffing pyramid. His own claim is that lower costs will activate projects clients previously deferred, narrowed or abandoned, while allowing firms to deliver higher-quality services. He applies the Jevons Paradox as the mechanism for this demand expansion.

pts.k: Wingens reports existing automation of document-intensive tasks and predicts greater economic viability for litigation and faster adoption of alternative fee arrangements.
pts.d: He describes LLM-assisted review of trust and servicing agreements, largely automated fund side-letter review, and AI searches across deposition transcripts. He argues that falling routine-work costs coexist with rising value for surrounding judgment. Extending this logic to discovery, he predicts that reduced document-review costs will make previously uneconomic middle-market disputes viable. As tools mature, he expects firms to share gains through fewer effective hours and value-linked alternative fee arrangements, not merely through hourly-rate reductions.

pts.k: Wingens predicts that clients' own AI-enabled productivity will generate additional transactional, intellectual-property, disputes and restructuring work.
pts.d: This is his second proposed demand mechanism, distinct from making existing legal needs cheaper to serve. He expects private fund managers to evaluate more opportunities and execute more transactions, technology and life sciences businesses to create more protectable intellectual property, and AI itself to generate disputes and eventual bankruptcy and restructuring work.

pts.k: Wingens acknowledges that in-house AI adoption will offset some external demand, but expects higher-stakes work to continue requiring firms' judgment.
pts.d: He predicts that corporate counsel will bring more routine work inside using the same legally trained AI tools available to firms. He characterizes most of this work as high-volume, low-judgment and already commoditizing. He nevertheless expects increased business activity to generate higher-stakes matters requiring seasoned judgment and private-market knowledge beyond what an AI agent alone supplies.

pts.k: Wingens predicts augmentation and earlier higher-value work for junior lawyers, with increased junior hiring conditional on demand outpacing automation.
pts.d: He concedes that senior lawyers can sometimes perform junior tasks themselves on smaller matters. On larger, more complex matters, he describes AI as a copilot that improves junior productivity, explains unfamiliar provisions or case theories, and supports training and work quality. His prediction that firms will need more juniors explicitly depends on demand rising faster than AI can absorb and juniors becoming capable of work previously requiring senior lawyers.

pts.k: Wingens expects proprietary firm knowledge and increasingly AI-native graduates to strengthen junior lawyers' capabilities.
pts.d: He envisages connecting associates to a curated precedent collection with tools highlighting deal terms and litigation strategies, giving them access to collective firm knowledge that clients cannot replicate. He predicts that proprietary knowledge will become more important as underlying models commoditize and that graduates will become increasingly native in AI technology over the next few years. He presents access to the precedent resource as an opportunity, rather than documenting measured results from its deployment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of firm experience, one quantified client-project anecdote, informal internal consultations and an economic analogy.
pts.d: Wingens reports current use cases in structured finance, funds and litigation. His principal numerical example is an unnamed project previously rejected on price: AI reduced its expected cost by roughly 70% despite higher hourly rates, and the firm obtained revenue while the client addressed risk at lower cost. The figure concerns expected project cost, not a measured firm-wide productivity or employment effect. He also reports asking counsel and associates about juniors' use of AI. The Jevons Paradox supplies a historical analogy for demand expansion. The article offers no systematic legal-market demand data, hiring series, model benchmarks or quantified quality outcomes; the broader demand, employment and training effects are Wingens's predictions and interpretations.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article combines reported current adoption with largely undated forecasts; expanded junior employment and improved training have explicit conditions.
pts.d: In the June 15, 2026 article, existing practice uses are described as already occurring, and the cost-reduction anecdote is dated to 'this past year' relative to publication. AI-native graduates are forecast over 'the next few years'; alternative pricing gains depend on tool maturation, and proprietary knowledge gains depend on model commoditization. Other demand forecasts have no precise horizon, with restructuring work described as arising 'ultimately.' Junior headcount expansion depends on demand outstripping AI capacity and juniors handling more senior-level work. Wingens explicitly requires independent thinking and questioning AI output, alongside active supervisor teaching, prompt sharing and explanation of matter structure. These are human oversight and learning conditions, not evidence of autonomous legal practice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects primarily concern business clients, corporate legal departments and law-firm lawyers, with different effects by task and matter complexity.
pts.d: Business clients gain lower costs and potentially higher quality, making previously unaffordable sophisticated work economically viable. Middle-market litigants may pursue meritorious disputes previously deterred by discovery costs. Private fund managers, technology companies and life sciences businesses generate additional legal needs through greater productivity. In-house counsel absorb routine tasks, partially reducing outside demand. Law firms gain potential new revenue and higher-judgment work; transactional, IP, litigation and restructuring practices are identified as beneficiaries. Juniors receive learning support and earlier higher-value assignments, with possible headcount growth subject to demand conditions. Seniors may take over some junior tasks on small matters and must actively train juniors. The discussion concerns commercial-service affordability rather than a specific claim about closing the civil access-to-justice gap.
